item.title: Bank of Canada set for pair of important data drops ahead of 'live' rate decision
item.description: The Bank of Canada will get a raft of fresh data to start next week as it weighs what could be a pivotal interest rate decision at the end of the month.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: OTTAWA -- The Bank of Canada will get a raft of fresh data to start next week as it weighs what could be a pivotal interest rate decision at the end of the month. Statistics Canada is set to release its September inflation data on Monday, giving the central bank a look at how energy price pressures are influencing other parts of the consumer basket. A Reuters poll of economists expects the annual rate of inflation rose to 3.2 per cent in September, up from three per cent in August, according to LSEG Data & Analytics. RBC assistant chief economist Nathan Janzen said he expects inflation held steady at three per cent last month. Persistently high gasoline prices tied to the ongoing war in Iran will remain the biggest fuel for inflation, he said. “We know that energy prices are high. What we don’t know yet is the extent that those higher energy prices have or are going to spill over to broader inflation pressures,” Janzen said. Economists at BMO are in line with the consensus expectations and call for inflation to be two tenths of a point higher in September, matching the fastest rate for inflation since December 2023. BMO’s Benjamin Reitzes and Shelly Kaushik said in a note to clients Friday that a 5.8 per cent monthly increase in gas prices and a double-digit hike in heating oil costs will fuel the jump. They expect some softness in travel and shelter prices to offset that increase. The Bank of Canada signalled at the start of the Middle East conflict last spring that it would look through a temporary rise in energy costs tied to the war. But officials have warned that the longer global oil prices remain high, the greater the risks that inflation spreads past the gas pump. In that case, the central bank could be forced to raise its policy rate, which has stood for nearly a year at 2.25 per cent. Most economists consider that level to be modestly stimulative to growth. Reitzes and Kaushik said they’re expecting the Bank of Canada’s preferred core inflation metrics to hold steady in September and are “not anticipating any red flags in this report.” Janzen said the Bank of Canada’s upcoming decision on Oct. 28 will be a “live” meeting, where the door is open for the central bank to raise its policy rate, but a hike is not his base case scenario. Even if the September price data shows signs inflationary pressures are spreading past the gas pumps, Janzen said the central bank will be weighing that against signs of softness in the labour market and wider economy. Statistics Canada reported last week that the economy shed 68,000 jobs in September, a second consecutive month of falling employment. A re-escalating trade dispute with the United States has also hampered growth prospects heading into the fourth quarter. “Higher energy prices -- all else equal -- would mean broader inflation pressures would be expected to rise in the future. But if the economy is getting weaker, then there are some offsetting disinflationary forces there as well,” Janzen said. “It puts (the Bank of Canada) still in a wait-and-see mode -- very, very data dependent.” Financial market odds of a quarter-point rate hike later this month fell after the weak September jobs report. Odds of a hike stood around 34 per cent as of Friday afternoon, according to LSEG Data & Analytics. Janzen said RBC’s call is for no rate hikes in 2026, with modest tightening starting next year. The Bank of Canada will also release its own quarterly surveys of businesses and consumers on Monday, which can give the bank a better sense of whether firms are planning to pass their own rising costs on to consumers. Janzen said inflation expectations and business confidence will help inform the central bank whether higher prices among producers could be passed on to store shelves in the months to come. --- Craig Lord, The Canadian Press This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 16, 2026.
